forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee prices will 'absolutely go down', he cites confidence in independent advice rather than giving the guarantee requested.

forthrightness.statement: don't have any expectation that the government would be putting capital up to actually build this. That would be the industry.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly clarifies who pays for construction in response to that line of questioning.

divination.statement: Reducing power spikes and lowering the risk premiums built into power bills will save Kiwis around 265 million dollars per year. That's equivalent of roughly $50 per household.
divination.explanation: A forecast of future savings dependent on commercial terms not yet concluded and on modelled 'downward pressure'; plausible but uncertain.

divination.statement: The government has shortlisted leading proposals and is now moving to commercial contracting with the aim of signing a contract to build by mid-2026. The facility will be operational as soon as 2027 or early 28.
divination.explanation: Predicts an operational date of 2027/early 2028 for a project still in commercial negotiation — infrastructure timelines of this kind frequently slip.

divination.statement: In the future, more than 95% of our electricity is expected to come from clean renewable energy.
divination.explanation: A directional forecast consistent with NZ's high renewable share and current trajectory, but the 95%+ level and timing are uncertain.

divination.statement: Access to LNG is also expected to protect around 2,000 jobs from the economic impact impacted by rising energy prices and gas shortages.
divination.explanation: A forward estimate of jobs protected; plausible but resting on modelled assumptions about future energy prices and gas supply.

divination.statement: The flow through in terms of the prices within the market do take some time to carry through, but the benefits that that have been articulated by the independent advice that I've received from my officials indicate that there will be a downward pressure on power prices.
divination.explanation: Predicts downward pressure on prices, directionally supported by the certainty rationale but with no committed timing or magnitude.

divination.statement: So the plant will be in play by winter 2027. So we will need to play that through.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the LNG/energy facility will be operational by winter 2027; a specific timeframe but an ambitious build schedule for a novel importation facility, so uncertain.

divination.statement: the future of the world is all about semiconductors and AI, but it's also going to be about the clean transition to clean energy and and a clean economy, and that's going to require EVs and solar panels. All of those source materials come from critical minerals, and that requires mining here in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecast that semiconductors, AI and clean-energy demand will drive critical-minerals need; directionally consistent with expert consensus, though 'requires mining here in New Zealand' is an assertion of necessity.

specificity.statement: So the plant will be in play by winter 2027. So we will need to play that through.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete date (winter 2027) but no detail on capacity, cost or mechanism.

specificity.statement: we've spoken to gene tailors in advance of the announcement today and everyone is on the same page that the capability that we're going to be putting in place in terms of energy security uh will have a downward pressure on price and we'll be watching that through the increase in regulation that we're putting in place through the electricity authority.
specificity.explanation: Points to a monitoring mechanism (Electricity Authority regulation) but no figures or enforcement detail.

specificity.statement: in our 2 years in government, uh we've actually got local water done well accelerated and and ready to go.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy but this line gives no figures or dates on its own.

specificity.statement: These are long run assets, 30, 50, 70 years. They need consistent annual investment in them. And secondarily, we want to make sure there's regulation to make sure they actually are spending money to make sure those assets are maintained in the appropriate way.
specificity.explanation: Names asset lifespans and two regulatory mechanisms (economic and quality), though without dollar figures.

forthrightness.statement: So the plant will be in play by winter 2027. So we will need to play that through.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether power prices will be cheaper next winter versus this winter; he pivots to when the plant will be operational and explicitly declines to guarantee, rather than answering the price comparison.

forthrightness.statement: we've spoken to gene tailors in advance of the announcement today and everyone is on the same page that the capability that we're going to be putting in place in terms of energy security uh will have a downward pressure on price and we'll be watching that through the increase in regulation that we're putting in place through the electricity authority.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether gentailers are on notice to pass savings through to households; he says they were consulted and shares his aim, but doesn't confirm any binding requirement to pass savings on.

forthrightness.statement: we have briefed the opposition parties in advance of this announcement this afternoon and we have provided officials to provide guidance to them in terms of what we're doing and why.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he'd assure the market the policy survives a change of government; he answers with the concrete step of briefing the opposition, though he can't guarantee their support.

forthrightness.statement: It's on the table.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked whether legislating consent is a yes or still on the table; he confirms it is 'on the table' but declines the yes/no, deferring a definitive answer to mid-year.

forthrightness.statement: the official advice uh, is is that uh, the uh, downward pressure in terms of the emissions profile uh, takes into account the aspects that are currently measured within the inventory at the moment. So, I'm happy to pick up the detail after that in regards to the point around the shipping point that you're raising.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether the quoted emissions numbers account for ~40% methane leakage in transport/storage; he answers only that figures cover what's 'currently measured in the inventory' and defers the actual question.

forthrightness.statement: As I understand it, it hasn't changed that materially from the same position last year versus this year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether ~50% of the Crown Regional Holdings book being at default risk is 'good enough'; he deflects to how the position compares year-on-year rather than judging whether it is acceptable.

forthrightness.statement: No, I haven't, but as I said, since we you know, the the construct for the Regional Infrastructure Fund is slightly different from the PGF, which was you know, we've got certainly it's almost exclusively loans.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether he'd spoken to Shane Jones; answers plainly 'No, I haven't' before contextualising.

forthrightness.statement: it's just I what I was reacting to, you know, um last weekend, I think it was, was just a presentation that is a fait accompli that we actually do have a deal with the Americans. We don't. Uh we have discussions that are ongoing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what role the US could have in mineral extraction; he corrects the premise and gives general context, though he avoids committing to specifics.

forthrightness.statement: Again, this is the point I've been trying to make over the last week. We're well ahead of ourselves here. We do not have a deal on the table with all of that detail on it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a specific conditional — whether US funding would mean exclusive mineral supply to the US; he declines to engage, repeating that it's premature. Arguably fair given no deal exists, but the question is not answered.

forthrightness.statement: Yeah, I I I I didn't because I don't need to. I was asked a straight-up question and I gave an answer and I'll continue to do that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he consulted the Minister of Foreign Affairs before calling on Trump to apologise; he directly admits he did not and explains why.

forthrightness.statement: Yeah, you know, we don't comment on on polls as you know. There's a lot of them and they say lots of different things at lots of different times.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the hung-parliament Curia poll means he's 'in trouble'; he deflects with the standard 'we don't comment on polls' line and never engages the question.

forthrightness.statement: We believe very strongly in media freedoms. So, we want to see that ruling and and that decision and understand that more before I comment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked his position on a Hong Kong ruling; states a general value (media freedom) but declines a substantive position, citing needing to read the decision — a reasonable but incomplete answer.

forthrightness.statement: I look, at the end of the day, uh it's the accountability of the councils uh have the shareholding or ownership of that entity uh to work through the investigation, work out uh what occurred.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the fact there were warning signs was acceptable; he sidesteps the acceptability judgement and redirects to council accountability and process.

forthrightness.statement: Uh so I'll be discussing those. I don't think it's appropriate to go into those options before we've had a discussion [cough] with the Mayor but under the Local Government Act the Minister of Local Government does have a range of powers to be able to provide intervention and support.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to share the other options on the table; he declines to list them pending the mayor meeting but gives a legitimate reason and gestures at the statutory basis, so a partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: Uh I remain confident that the council and the entities involved are doing what they are required to do in the context of the transition to the Local Water Done Well structure.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether he has confidence in the chair of Wellington Water; he expresses confidence in 'the council and the entities' generally, not the chair, partly evading the pointed question.

veracity.explanation: Unfalsifiable from the text — asserts officials' conclusion without the evidence, so cannot be verified.

veracity.explanation: Mill closures and job losses tied to high power prices did occur, but attributing them solely to the previous government's lack of energy policy oversimplifies contested causation (global gas prices, Pohokura decline).

veracity.statement: the biggest risk in this particular market of New Zealand, different from other countries around the world, is dry dry dry year risk.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — NZ's heavy reliance on hydro makes dry-year (low lake inflow) risk a genuine and distinctive feature of its electricity market.

veracity.statement: just sitting on our hands like the Labour government did for six years and created the problem that we inherited. Well, we're cleaning up that mess and so um, we'll make no apologies for pushing forward and getting things done.

veracity.statement: We've been talking about this since Havelock North, like 10 years ago, and people have been sitting on their hands.
veracity.explanation: The Havelock North campylobacter outbreak was 2016 (~10 years), a fair reference point for water-infrastructure concern; 'sitting on their hands' is a rhetorical overstatement.

veracity.statement: As I understand it, it hasn't changed that materially from the same position last year versus this year.
veracity.explanation: Comparative claim about the book's risk being materially unchanged; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.explanation: States plainly there is no deal with the US, only ongoing discussions — a truthful correction of the premise, consistent with the early stage of any critical-minerals arrangement.

civility.explanation: Partisan blame of the previous government; frames it around policy but assigns responsibility for job losses in a pointed, accusatory way.

civility.statement: if we have to pass legislation to do it, we will do it. Because we're not prepared to have New Zealand consumers paying higher electricity prices they need to because we can't organize an energy policy uh, which is what the Labour government showed us last time.
civility.explanation: Renewed partisan swipe at the previous government's competence woven into a policy point.

civility.statement: just sitting on our hands like the Labour government did for six years and created the problem that we inherited. Well, we're cleaning up that mess and so um, we'll make no apologies for pushing forward and getting things done.
civility.explanation: Us-vs-them 'cleaning up their mess' framing; blames predecessors rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: We've been talking about this since Havelock North, like 10 years ago, and people have been sitting on their hands.
civility.explanation: General 'people sitting on their hands' criticism directed at prior inaction, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: when you look at the reality of the impact of what this has had on local communities and and Wellingtonians, you know, it's completely unacceptable. And uh you know, I uh I acknowledge the work that the that the mayor has taken. He's new into the role,
civility.explanation: Focuses on the impact and acknowledges the new mayor's work; respectful and cooperative in tone rather than attacking.

charisma.statement: we have briefed the opposition parties in advance of this announcement this afternoon and we have provided officials to provide guidance to them in terms of what we're doing and why.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building — reaching across to opposition parties and offering officials, seeking cross-party continuity rather than confrontation.

charisma.statement: when you look at the reality of the impact of what this has had on local communities and and Wellingtonians, you know, it's completely unacceptable. And uh you know, I uh I acknowledge the work that the that the mayor has taken. He's new into the role,
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory and collaborative — acknowledges the mayor and offers central-government support, building rather than dividing.

strength.statement: if we have to pass legislation to do it, we will do it. Because we're not prepared to have New Zealand consumers paying higher electricity prices they need to because we can't organize an energy policy uh, which is what the Labour government showed us last time.
strength.explanation: Commitment to legislate if needed, backed by a track record cited (fast-track); but the specific facility is not yet delivered, so it remains stated intent.

strength.statement: You've seen us do it with fast track. Uh, we have to speed things up in this country and so um, we need to get to yes much, much quicker.
strength.explanation: Cites the fast-track legislation his government actually passed as evidence of delivery capability — a real enacted policy supporting the claim.

strength.statement: in our 2 years in government, uh we've actually got local water done well accelerated and and ready to go.
strength.explanation: Local Water Done Well legislation was passed and entities are transitioning (1 July date cited) — genuine, partial delivery in progress rather than mere announcement.

authenticity.statement: You've seen us do it with fast track. Uh, we have to speed things up in this country and so um, we need to get to yes much, much quicker.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the government's record: it did legislate the Fast-track Approvals Act, so the appeal to prior action is broadly backed by deeds.

specificity.statement: although the PM has identified diesel as the source of the major problem... we've got complaints coming from the forestry sector that they're slowing down, with farmers doing the haka that they can't um develop and create the necessary export output. So, that's why I'm focused on the diesel. Kā Noa and MBIE are bringing back a proposal. The moment it passes muster, we will announce it, the final storage and the financial amount.
specificity.explanation: Names the fuel type (diesel), the sector, and the agencies (Kā Noa, MBIE), but defers the actual storage volume and financial amount to a later announcement.

specificity.statement: at the moment we hold tickets to different types of crude oil, as well as some refined products. Uh we have assessed those, and very few of them are actually suitable for use in New Zealand. So, the unsolicited proposal that we've had is from a commercial entity that has basically said, "Let's do a swap. We'll exchange you what you've got an option on in exchange for a particular volume of refined fuel that could be used in New Zealand."
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism concretely: IEA tickets on crude/refined product, suitability assessment, and a swap-for-usable-fuel deal.

specificity.statement: Treasury, like just about every economist in the world right now, caviats every piece of advice they give me by saying it depends how long this conflict lasts... in the latest scenarios, in which they take into account a longer uh conflict with deeper disruption to supply chains, they have inflation uh peaking higher uh than I previously presented to you.
specificity.explanation: Directional ('peaking higher') but provides no figure, timeframe, or magnitude.

specificity.statement: They have given me a range of numbers, and I'm not going to share them because they haven't landed on a final scenario, nor even a central scenario... they think inflation will go much higher this year and it will stay out of our target band.
specificity.explanation: 'Out of our target band' is somewhat concrete, but no figure or timing is given.

specificity.statement: officials have provided me formal advice because they agree with you that two two triggers have been have had have had changes... their advice assessing all of those changes together including information that we have against the other criteria is that there is no material development in the risk to fuel supply... I've agreed with them and we're not scheduling a meeting. But the reason we've made those assessment criteria transparent is so that people can see when they are being brought into issue.
specificity.explanation: References the concrete triggers (three-day jet-fuel reduction, Australian policy change) and the published assessment criteria.

specificity.statement: we're just acknowledging anecdotal evidence that we've seen you know some hoarding take place by some people. specificity.explanation: Vague on scale ('a few localized places', 'some rural communities'); the allocation-policy change is mentioned but not detailed here.

specificity.statement: we've heard reports out of Port Waikato, Southland, Nelson where at various times there have been what sometimes referred to as a stockout... in order to deal with imbalances across the country... they have changed their systems to go from one month to one week. And of course that alters how much supply you can get at one time... If we do see major issues like this continuing to escalate, that would be a trigger for assessing a move in the fuel plan.
specificity.explanation: Names specific regions and the precise mechanism (distributors moving ordering cycles from monthly to weekly) driving stockouts.

specificity.statement: I'd say we're doing everything needed to protect our fuel security for the future. But actually there's a limit to how much storage we have now. So, stopping fuel flowing wouldn't necessarily put us in a better position.
specificity.explanation: 'Everything needed' is a platitude, but the storage-limit point adds some concrete substance.

specificity.statement: our advice is pretty clear. It's poorly targeted. It actually benefits high-income households and it actually encourages fuel use when it's constrained. specificity.explanation: Offers criteria (targeted, temporary, timely; benefits high-income) but no dollar figures or design detail.

specificity.explanation: Describes graduated priority bands and a continued price mechanism, though without detailing the bands themselves.

specificity.statement: that's why we're being upfront that we have received these proposals, that we're now officially calling for proposals, so that any proposals can be tested against the same fair set of criteria uh according to the goals that we've set out, which is securing fuel supply above and beyond that which would otherwise occur through commercial arrangements in a way that minimizes risk to the crown.
specificity.explanation: States the goal and the fair-criteria/open-call mechanism, though the criteria themselves aren't enumerated here.

specificity.explanation: Mostly thematic ('real world', 'calm, measured', 'not COVID 2.0') with no concrete measures or figures.

specificity.explanation: Cites geothermal/solar/wind investment and a concrete 2024 spot-price figure (~$800/MWh) tied to job losses.

specificity.statement: the maximum rebate will gradually reduce for families earning more than $140,000 a year up to the limit of $180,000.
specificity.explanation: Names exact abatement thresholds ($140k–$180k), a precise targeting mechanism.

specificity.statement: Household income will be calculated by Inland Revenue using the past 3 months' worth of actual reported income to determine eligibility.
specificity.explanation: Specifies the administering agency, the data used, and the assessment window.

specificity.statement: In our campaign, we wished to directly reimburse parents every fortnight for 25% of their early childhood education costs. However, on entering office, officials advised us that the systems simply aren't sophisticated enough to deliver it that way.
specificity.explanation: Contrasts the specific original design against the reason for change, though the systems limitation is described only generally.

specificity.statement: The advice we received was that it would take 2 to 3 years to deliver. Our view is that that's simply too long to wait. Families need relief this year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe (2–3 years) and a target (relief this year).

specificity.statement: Family Boost will make a difference to more than 100,000 Kiwi families. That's 140,000 New Zealand children.
specificity.explanation: Concrete beneficiary figures for families and children.

specificity.statement: Families who qualify for the maximum reimbursement will receive $975 in their bank accounts in October and then another $975 every 3 months thereafter.
specificity.explanation: Exact amount, start month, and recurrence — precise and checkable.

specificity.statement: the advice we've received is that the mean income uh for families with young children, if you judge it on uh the families receiving the Best Start tax credit, is expected to be $114,000 in the 2025 income tax year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure with a defined population basis (Best Start recipients) and tax year.

specificity.statement: I can confirm that based on official modeling, around 21,000 families would be entitled to the full payment.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure sourced to official modelling.

specificity.statement: what I wanted was for the IRD to simply put this money into people's bank accounts, but they advised us they could not do that without building a new system that would take 2 to 3 years.
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism (photo/upload invoice to IRD) and the 2–3 year alternative timeframe.

specificity.statement: one of the challenges in implementing this policy has been that the government does not collect fees data about early childhood providers. One of the advantages of this policy is that we will now be able to collect that data every quarter when parents submit their invoices.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete data gap and how the scheme will fill it (quarterly invoice data).

specificity.statement: we've costed the policy on 100% uptake. And the reason for that is I want every single family who is eligible for this support to get it.
specificity.explanation: Concrete costing assumption (100% uptake) tied to a clear intent.

specificity.statement: what I can tell you is the minister and myself are actually really focused and very fixated on making sure we get maximum learning out of out of the events. That's why once we digest these two reports, we're up for actioning you know, recommendations that are there.

specificity.statement: We've been clear that the coalition agreements we've made with coalition partners have changed the shape of the policies that National campaigned on. specificity.explanation: Names the goal (fiscally neutral tax reduction) but withholds the concrete allowance numbers asked for.

specificity.statement: we won't fix everything in one budget, you know, after 6 years of mismanagement. strength.statement: Over the last two years our government has focused on getting inflation down, easing pressure on interest rates, keeping taxes low and restoring discipline to government spending.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a record of delivery; some measures (tax settings, spending restraint) were enacted, but framed as ongoing effort rather than a single delivered outcome.

strength.statement: We are committed to returning the books to surplus by 2028-2029 and putting debt on a downward path towards 40% of GDP.
strength.explanation: A restated fiscal commitment; delivery is future-dated and in-progress, not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: it's why we've reversed the oil and gas exploration ban and it's why we have a procurement process underway for imported LNG.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete action: the exploration-ban reversal was legislated by the government, while LNG procurement is described as merely 'underway' rather than delivered.

strength.statement: So, Minister Brown and I will be bringing legislation into Parliament to provide the government with the capacity to require information from both the users of the residual gas resource and the producers.
strength.explanation: An announcement of a bill not yet introduced or passed; delivery remains to be seen.

veracity.statement: In April our total exports reached 8.6 billion dollars up 943 million dollars or 12% on the same month last year. Our trade surplus in April was the largest on record at 1.92 billion dollars.
veracity.explanation: Precise, falsifiable figures presented as official trade data; internally consistent (943m ≈ 12%) and plausible, but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: new figures showing almost 360,000 international visitors arrived in March, up 15% on the same time last year. And new figures show we welcomed 3.63 million international visitors in the year ending March, and that was up 9.2% on the previous year.
veracity.explanation: Specific visitor figures presented as official statistics; plausible post-COVID recovery numbers but unverifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: the net operating package will be $2.1 billion, around $300 million lower than the allowance set in December.
veracity.explanation: Concrete pre-budget signalling figure, consistent internally, but a forward statement not yet confirmed by the budget itself.

veracity.statement: The previous government's decision to ban oil and gas exploration has left those businesses high and dry.
veracity.explanation: The 2018 exploration ban plausibly contributed to reduced gas investment, but attributing current business hardship solely to it omits other supply and market factors.

veracity.statement: Look, that's a provisional number. It's very difficult to estimate what if any losses will occur. With the the most recent example we have is the North Island weather event scheme which so far has lent, I think, approximately $1.7 billion. The losses on that scheme so far are only $2 million.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures for the weather-event scheme presented as fact; plausible and internally coherent but unverifiable here, and 'so far' appropriately hedges.

veracity.statement: As a result of Labour's reckless oil and gas ban, recent figures show New Zealand's gas reserves at January 1 were 731 petajoules, a decrease a decrease of 217 petajoules or 23% on last year's figures.
veracity.explanation: The reserve figures and decline are specific and plausible, but attributing the entire fall to the exploration ban ignores that reserves fall through extraction and reclassification too.

veracity.statement: EECA estimates that if the full 1.2 billion dollars of lending goes ahead, up to 10 petajoules of gas use could be reduced each year by using alternative energy sources.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to an EECA estimate and hedged with 'up to'; reasonable but unverified.

veracity.statement: Since 2023, we've suffered a drop from 148 petajoules down to 85. A loss of 43% of known gas resource.
veracity.explanation: Figures are internally consistent (148→85 ≈ 43%) and presented as factual; plausible but unverifiable and the metric differs from Brown's 731 PJ reserve figure without reconciliation.

veracity.statement: we're on the verge of signing 100 million deals to spend genuine Pūtea... to invest and continue to expand known fields. They walked away from it and they continued to tell me, Nicola, and the Prime Minister, they are not coming back.
veracity.explanation: A first-hand account of investors withdrawing near-signed deals; plausible but a self-reported narrative with no corroborating detail offered.

forthrightness.statement: Well, look, we uh always said in our government when any business is forced to close due to not being viable anymore, our job is to look at what are the underlying conditions in which businesses operate and we have been 100% on the case of energy affordability.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly why he did not step in to stop specific mills (e.g. Otahuhu) closing last year, he pivots to generalities about 'underlying conditions' and blame rather than answering the specific inaction.

forthrightness.statement: Because I'm not replacing the role of the bank. I don't think that government is well equipped to get in there and look at the balance sheets and profit and loss records of every business in New Zealand. That is the role for commercial banks who are best placed to make those judgments. What the Crown can do is step in to reduce the cost of that lending with its backing, with its guarantee.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the ideological question about why she accepts Crown intervention here but not before, drawing the distinction between guaranteeing loans and being the lender.

forthrightness.statement: Look, that's a provisional number. It's very difficult to estimate what if any losses will occur. With the the most recent example we have is the North Island weather event scheme which so far has lent, I think, approximately $1.7 billion. The losses on that scheme so far are only $2 million.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the challenge about taxpayers losing $48m, explaining it is a provisional ceiling and citing a comparable scheme's low actual losses.

forthrightness.statement: Oh, well, I don't think you're comparing apples with apples... the banks will do the due diligence, the banks will wear part of the loss, and the Crown will be the last woman standing. And sure, it's a risk, but it's something that we feel is a reasonable thing to do because we want these firms to continue to flourish.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he can be sure the $1.2b will return given the PGF's ~10% return record, he deflects the comparison but does explain the risk-sharing mechanism and concedes 'it's a risk'.

forthrightness.statement: I don't think it's fair to say that the owners of the gas resource, in the sense of those who are investing in it, are not telling us the truth. But, we do need greater surveillance powers within the state to ascertain what is happening with the diminishing resource we have.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to whether the industry's information can be trusted after being badly wrong three years ago; defends the industry's honesty while justifying new information powers, though he doesn't fully address why the earlier estimates were so off.

civility.statement: The truth is we have been left with a electricity system severely damaged by the last government's reckless decisions to prioritize wearing a climate change badge over New Zealand's affordable energy needs.
civility.explanation: Attributes motive ('wearing a climate change badge') to opponents rather than engaging the policy substance; 'reckless' and the badge jibe are pointed characterisations.

civility.statement: The previous government's decision to ban oil and gas exploration has left those businesses high and dry.
civility.explanation: Criticises an opponent's policy decision rather than the person, though 'high and dry' is a pointed characterisation.

civility.statement: the GIDI fund was hundreds of millions of dollars handed out willy-nilly at the behest of a minister. This is commercial banks determining who is creditworthy and making loans so that firms can invest their own money in the transition. So, this is not letting businesses off the hook for their own investments as the GIDI fund was doing.
civility.explanation: 'Willy-nilly' and 'at the behest of a minister' are barbed but target the design of a policy rather than a person.

civility.statement: As a result of Labour's reckless oil and gas ban, recent figures show New Zealand's gas reserves at January 1 were 731 petajoules, a decrease a decrease of 217 petajoules or 23% on last year's figures.
civility.explanation: 'Labour's reckless... ban' is a partisan tag, though attached to a policy critique rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I don't think it's fair to say that the owners of the gas resource, in the sense of those who are investing in it, are not telling us the truth. But, we do need greater surveillance powers within the state to ascertain what is happening with the diminishing resource we have.
civility.explanation: Declines to impugn the gas producers' honesty and frames the issue around information rather than blame.

rigor.statement: The truth is we have been left with a electricity system severely damaged by the last government's reckless decisions to prioritize wearing a climate change badge over New Zealand's affordable energy needs.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a single-cause link between prior policy and current damage with no evidence, and imputes motive rather than reasoning from data.

rigor.statement: As I said last week, when Kiwi businesses do well, New Zealanders do well. Successful businesses create jobs and pay higher wages that make life more affordable and give people more choices.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable causal direction but asserted as truism without evidence.

rigor.statement: The previous government's decision to ban oil and gas exploration has left those businesses high and dry.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause attribution of business distress to one policy, without weighing other contributors.

rigor.statement: I support government intervention in businesses or markets when it is very well targeted and where there is a compelling case to achieve broader economic objectives. The gas situation in New Zealand today meets that criteria.
rigor.explanation: States a conditional test and asserts it is met; reasoning is coherent but the 'compelling case' is claimed rather than demonstrated here.

rigor.statement: Because I'm not replacing the role of the bank. I don't think that government is well equipped to get in there and look at the balance sheets and profit and loss records of every business in New Zealand. That is the role for commercial banks who are best placed to make those judgments. What the Crown can do is step in to reduce the cost of that lending with its backing, with its guarantee.
rigor.explanation: Clear logical distinction between a loan guarantee and direct lending/grant-making, with the conclusion following from that premise.

rigor.statement: Look, that's a provisional number. It's very difficult to estimate what if any losses will occur. With the the most recent example we have is the North Island weather event scheme which so far has lent, I think, approximately $1.7 billion. The losses on that scheme so far are only $2 million.
rigor.explanation: Uses an analogous prior scheme as evidence that provisioned losses tend to exceed realised losses; reasonable but a single analogy.

rigor.statement: the GIDI fund was hundreds of millions of dollars handed out willy-nilly at the behest of a minister. This is commercial banks determining who is creditworthy and making loans so that firms can invest their own money in the transition. So, this is not letting businesses off the hook for their own investments as the GIDI fund was doing.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent grants-vs-guarantee distinction, though 'willy-nilly' is a rhetorical characterisation rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: As a result of Labour's reckless oil and gas ban, recent figures show New Zealand's gas reserves at January 1 were 731 petajoules, a decrease a decrease of 217 petajoules or 23% on last year's figures.
rigor.explanation: Causal attribution of the reserve drop to one policy ('as a result of') without accounting for depletion or downgrades.

rigor.statement: Oh, well, I don't think you're comparing apples with apples... the banks will do the due diligence, the banks will wear part of the loss, and the Crown will be the last woman standing. And sure, it's a risk, but it's something that we feel is a reasonable thing to do because we want these firms to continue to flourish.
rigor.explanation: Explains the bank due-diligence and loss-sharing structure, but the PGF comparison is dismissed rather than rebutted with data.

rigor.statement: we're on the verge of signing 100 million deals to spend genuine Pūtea... to invest and continue to expand known fields. They walked away from it and they continued to tell me, Nicola, and the Prime Minister, they are not coming back.
rigor.explanation: Personal testimony used to argue policy uncertainty deters investment; reasonable but rests on anecdote rather than documented evidence.

divination.statement: EECA estimates that if the full 1.2 billion dollars of lending goes ahead, up to 10 petajoules of gas use could be reduced each year by using alternative energy sources.
divination.explanation: A conditional forecast of annual gas-use reduction; plausible as an agency estimate but 'up to' and 'if the full amount' make the realised figure uncertain.

divination.statement: You heard what I said about 85 petajoules. 2030, one forecast scenario is 50 petajoules. 2036, 25 petajoules.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a steep gas-reserve decline to 2030 and 2036; directionally consistent with depletion trends but flagged as 'one forecast scenario', so the specific figures are uncertain.

veracity.statement: the oil and gas ban sent an absolutely chilling effect through international investors to say New Zealand is not open for business. We do not welcome your hundreds of millions of dollars worth of capital for exploration, and that had what we call a chilling effect on the global investor community.
veracity.explanation: The 2018 exploration ban's effect on investment is contested; some withdrawal occurred but the sweeping 'chilling effect' framing is an exaggeration of a mixed, hard-to-quantify picture.

veracity.statement: stopping Labour's Lake Onslow boondoggle, which put a chilling impact on other investors to put in place renewable power. We removed that.
veracity.explanation: The government did cancel the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme; the claim it deterred private renewable investment is a defensible but contested interpretation.

veracity.statement: We got rid of the 2030 100% renewable energy target, which was saying don't don't invest in thermal firming, which also stopped renewable projects from going ahead because without firming those projects aren't actually viable.
veracity.explanation: The government did move away from the 2030 100% renewable target; the causal claim that the target itself blocked renewable projects via firming is a plausible but arguable interpretation.

veracity.statement: We also did the 20-year deal with Tiwai, which has unlocked further generation by providing certainty to the market.
veracity.explanation: A long-term Tiwai Point smelter electricity deal was signed, consistent with this claim; the 'unlocked further generation' effect is directionally supported.

veracity.statement: all of that has seen wholesale prices for electricity drop significantly this year. They're down $30 for a megawatt hour since since February.
veracity.explanation: A specific quantitative claim; wholesale prices are volatile and seasonal, so a February-to-now fall is plausible but the attribution to policy and the exact $30 figure are uncertain.

veracity.statement: we live in a country that last quarter, I think, ran at 98% renewable electricity.
veracity.explanation: New Zealand's renewable electricity share is typically ~80-90%; 98% for a full quarter would be unusually high and likely overstates the figure, though a wet, high-hydro quarter could approach it.

veracity.statement: Fast track has seen the largest wind farm in New Zealand recently consented in Southland.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with a large Southland wind farm being consented via the fast-track regime; broadly checkable and plausible.

authenticity.statement: the oil and gas ban sent an absolutely chilling effect through international investors to say New Zealand is not open for business. We do not welcome your hundreds of millions of dollars worth of capital for exploration, and that had what we call a chilling effect on the global investor community.
authenticity.explanation: National consistently opposed the ban in opposition and is now acting to reverse it, so the rhetoric is consistent with the party's long-held position and current policy.

specificity.statement: the oil and gas ban sent an absolutely chilling effect through international investors to say New Zealand is not open for business. We do not welcome your hundreds of millions of dollars worth of capital for exploration, and that had what we call a chilling effect on the global investor community.
specificity.explanation: Repeats the 'chilling effect' metaphor and gestures at 'hundreds of millions' but names no figures, firms, or evidence.

specificity.statement: we're putting $200 million aside to co-invest with potential explorers of gas here in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete dollar figure ($200m) and a specific mechanism (co-investment with explorers), though timeframe is unstated.

specificity.statement: stopping Labour's Lake Onslow boondoggle, which put a chilling impact on other investors to put in place renewable power. We removed that.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project and the action taken, but not the scale or the investors affected.

specificity.statement: We also did the 20-year deal with Tiwai, which has unlocked further generation by providing certainty to the market.
specificity.explanation: Names the counterparty and 20-year term, but not the price or generation figures involved.

specificity.statement: all of that has seen wholesale prices for electricity drop significantly this year. They're down $30 for a megawatt hour since since February.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise figure ($30/MWh) and reference point (since February).

specificity.statement: we live in a country that last quarter, I think, ran at 98% renewable electricity.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise percentage and timeframe, hedged with 'I think'.

specificity.statement: Fast track has seen the largest wind farm in New Zealand recently consented in Southland.
specificity.explanation: Names the project type, location and superlative but no capacity figure or name.

specificity.statement: I believe they've got to make a minimum of 15% reduction in gas. It might be that they invest in more efficient plant and equipment, so they still use gas, but they become more efficient in their use of gas.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete eligibility threshold (minimum 15% gas reduction) and mechanism, hedged with 'I believe'.

specificity.statement: This is not replacing. This is new infrastructure... So, as as Shane said, if you're a bakery uh you know, producing you know, lots of bread, uh you need gas. That's what they've written to us and said. So, this is actually about protecting what is remaining of the gas as as those gas fields decline
specificity.explanation: Uses a concrete example (a bakery needing gas) but gives no actual advice or rule for new builds as asked.

civility.statement: the oil and gas ban sent an absolutely chilling effect through international investors to say New Zealand is not open for business. We do not welcome your hundreds of millions of dollars worth of capital for exploration, and that had what we call a chilling effect on the global investor community.
civility.explanation: Criticises a policy rather than a person, though the loaded 'chilling effect' framing leans rhetorical.

civility.statement: stopping Labour's Lake Onslow boondoggle, which put a chilling impact on other investors to put in place renewable power. We removed that.
civility.explanation: 'Boondoggle' is a dismissive label for an opponent's policy, but the criticism targets the project not a person.

strength.statement: we're putting $200 million aside to co-invest with potential explorers of gas here in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: A concrete funding commitment but at announcement stage; delivery and uptake by explorers are not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: stopping Labour's Lake Onslow boondoggle, which put a chilling impact on other investors to put in place renewable power. We removed that.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered action (cancelling the project) that the government actually carried out.

strength.statement: We got rid of the 2030 100% renewable energy target, which was saying don't don't invest in thermal firming, which also stopped renewable projects from going ahead because without firming those projects aren't actually viable.
strength.explanation: A concrete policy change the government actually enacted.

strength.statement: We also did the 20-year deal with Tiwai, which has unlocked further generation by providing certainty to the market.
strength.explanation: A concrete, completed agreement rather than an aspiration, delivered under this government.

strength.statement: all of that has seen wholesale prices for electricity drop significantly this year. They're down $30 for a megawatt hour since since February.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered outcome, but credits a bundle of policies for a market movement that also reflects seasonal supply.

strength.statement: Fast track has seen the largest wind farm in New Zealand recently consented in Southland.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete consenting outcome under the government's fast-track policy, though consent is not yet built generation.

rigor.statement: We cannot have national security in a volatile world if we do not have more energy independence. And that's why we're actually up for doing everything we can around thermal energy, around renewable energy, and this is part of that process.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable premise-to-conclusion link between energy independence and security, but asserted rather than evidenced and framed broadly ('everything we can').

rigor.statement: We got rid of the 2030 100% renewable energy target, which was saying don't don't invest in thermal firming, which also stopped renewable projects from going ahead because without firming those projects aren't actually viable.
rigor.explanation: Offers a logical chain (no firming → projects unviable → renewables stall) but supports it with assertion rather than data.

rigor.statement: the reality is this is a decision made by cabinet, period. And there was a lot of us as cabinet ministers coming into the cabinet room even well before this issue... with very strong views on the subject that when you're talking about climate change frameworks, they're built up by governments over many years. And actually, it's the state's responsibility. It's not the courts or businesses.
rigor.explanation: Presents a coherent argument that climate frameworks are the state's responsibility not the courts', though it is asserted rather than evidenced.

charisma.statement: We cannot have national security in a volatile world if we do not have more energy independence. And that's why we're actually up for doing everything we can around thermal energy, around renewable energy, and this is part of that process.
charisma.explanation: Confident framing that reframes energy around national security, but appeals to its own side's priorities rather than seeking cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: We'd all love to be 100% renewables, but the reality is we're going to need gas and transition fuels for some time in our system.
charisma.explanation: 'We'd all love to be 100% renewables' briefly acknowledges the shared aspiration before pivoting, a mild bridge-building gesture.

forthrightness.statement: Well, our entire policies have been around how do we make sure that wholesale electricity prices are more competitive and more affordable? And that's where making sure we have a security of supply and reliable electricity is is critically important.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether any modelling was done on the grid/household impact of transitioning off gas, he pivots to general talking points about affordability and never says whether modelling exists.

forthrightness.statement: But your your question is is this going to increase the power price? No, the price of electricity, no, it won't. It will support uh businesses to be able to transition and we have a we have a significant build out of generation currently underway
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct yes/no ('no, it won't') to the question of whether the policy will raise power prices, though he offers no modelling to back the assurance.

forthrightness.statement: Well, yes, this is about protecting jobs, particularly in regional and rural New Zealand. And no, this is not about this will not this will not be increasing power prices.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers both parts of a two-part question with a clear 'yes' (protects jobs) and 'no' (won't raise prices).

forthrightness.statement: the reality is this is a decision made by cabinet, period. And there was a lot of us as cabinet ministers coming into the cabinet room even well before this issue... with very strong views on the subject that when you're talking about climate change frameworks, they're built up by governments over many years. And actually, it's the state's responsibility. It's not the courts or businesses.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a review into lobbyists giving his staff documents, he redirects to defending the merits of the Smith v Fonterra cabinet decision rather than addressing the process concern raised.

forthrightness.statement: Look, all I know is that we've got no no no no no recollection, no record of of the interaction back in 2024. I know my office has reached out to ministerial services and said, "Hey, you know, ideally we should have that." And as a result, reminding everybody of their obligations.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially answers what he knows (no recollection or record of the 2024 interaction) but quickly deflects back to the broader case rather than detailing what happened in his office.

forthrightness.statement: I just say to you, I think the person who's going to win Napier is going to be Katie Nimon. So, that's a very hypothetical question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd have Stuart Nash in a future cabinet, he dodges by predicting the electorate result and labelling the question hypothetical rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: This is not replacing. This is new infrastructure... So, as as Shane said, if you're a bakery uh you know, producing you know, lots of bread, uh you need gas. That's what they've written to us and said. So, this is actually about protecting what is remaining of the gas as as those gas fields decline
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd advise businesses and homeowners against new gas infrastructure, he avoids a yes/no and pivots to protecting existing gas for businesses that need it.

divination.statement: But your your question is is this going to increase the power price? No, the price of electricity, no, it won't. It will support uh businesses to be able to transition and we have a we have a significant build out of generation currently underway
divination.explanation: Predicts the policy will not increase electricity prices; optimistic and asserted without supporting modelling, so accuracy is uncertain.

divination.statement: We'd all love to be 100% renewables, but the reality is we're going to need gas and transition fuels for some time in our system.
divination.explanation: Predicts continued reliance on gas/transition fuels for years; consistent with most expert energy-system analyses for New Zealand's firming needs.

divination.statement: I just say to you, I think the person who's going to win Napier is going to be Katie Nimon. So, that's a very hypothetical question.
divination.explanation: Predicts Katie Nimon will win Napier; a plausible but genuinely uncertain electoral forecast that partisanship inclines him to make.

veracity.statement: Some 27 of the 49 action points on that list have now been completed, and this week in the house we continue that work.
veracity.explanation: A checkable progress claim about the 100-day plan; broadly consistent with the government's published tracker at the time.

veracity.statement: work-ready job seekers are now projected to spend an average of 13 years on a benefit. And that teenagers who go on to welfare will become trapped there for an average of 24 years of their working life.
veracity.explanation: Cites MSD lifetime-liability projections, but presents forecast modelling as settled fact; the figures are contested and context-dependent.

veracity.statement: a teenager who becomes trapped on welfare now may not get their first job until they're 40 because of how broken the welfare system has become under labor.
veracity.explanation: Misleading use of an average to imply a first job only at 40; overstated.

veracity.statement: Current modeling shows young people who spend almost their entire working lives on a main benefit could end up costing the taxpayer nearly a million dollars each in future payments.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with worst-case lifetime-cost modelling but applies an extreme scenario as a headline figure.

veracity.statement: there's been a 57% increase in the number of people on jobseeker benefits, right? And it's gone up 70,000 people over the course of the last 6 years. At the same time, we know there's been about a 58% reduction in actually uh sanctions being applied.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker numbers did rise materially and sanctions did fall over the period; the specific percentages are in the plausible range but presented without base context.

veracity.statement: your average time on a jobseeker benefit has gone from 10 and 1/2 years to 13 years under this under the last government. On the same hand, you've actually got young people receiving benefit payments who are now languishing on benefits for 24 years on average. That is up over 50% and a very in 3 years.
veracity.explanation: Quotes projection figures as realised facts; the direction is defensible but the presentation overstates certainty.

veracity.statement: This is expected to result in an additional 2 and 1/2 thousand job seekers each month having a work testable activity to [check in] on what they have been doing.
veracity.explanation: A forward estimate presented with appropriate hedging ('expected to').

veracity.statement: I believe the previous minister set the tone for a lighter touch to benefit sanctions by saying they needed to be used and I quote sparingly and as a last resort. I believe this has hindered MSD's efforts to shift some people off welfare and into work.
veracity.explanation: The attributed quote reflects the prior minister's stated stance; the causal claim about hindering MSD is her inference.

veracity.statement: With 70,000 more people now on job seeker support compared to when National left office 6 years ago. And about 40,000 more people have been receiving the support for a year or more.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker rolls and long-duration numbers did grow over the period; figures are in the plausible range but omit the Covid context.

veracity.statement: the um MSD evidence from February 2010 um draws on some of the OECD evidence as well. It actually says the use of sanctions and the threat of sanctions does actually improve work exits.
veracity.explanation: Fairly characterises one older evidence base, but selectively favours it over the more recent NZ-specific 2018 finding raised by the reporter.

veracity.statement: One of the biggest ones is that 60% of children who are in material hardship are in benefit dependent homes.
veracity.explanation: A specific statistic that is contestable; the share of children in hardship in benefit-reliant homes is high but the exact figure and framing are debatable.

specificity.statement: Some 27 of the 49 action points on that list have now been completed, and this week in the house we continue that work.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures (27 of 49) and a timeframe (this week).

specificity.statement: work-ready job seekers are now projected to spend an average of 13 years on a benefit. And that teenagers who go on to welfare will become trapped there for an average of 24 years of their working life.
specificity.explanation: Precise averages (13 years, 24 years) tied to defined groups.

specificity.statement: Current modeling shows young people who spend almost their entire working lives on a main benefit could end up costing the taxpayer nearly a million dollars each in future payments.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figure and defined cohort.

specificity.statement: there's been a 57% increase in the number of people on jobseeker benefits, right? And it's gone up 70,000 people over the course of the last 6 years. At the same time, we know there's been about a 58% reduction in actually uh sanctions being applied.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: your average time on a jobseeker benefit has gone from 10 and 1/2 years to 13 years under this under the last government. On the same hand, you've actually got young people receiving benefit payments who are now languishing on benefits for 24 years on average. That is up over 50% and a very in 3 years.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures and a percentage change.

specificity.statement: Well, it'd be a good start. I mean, what we've seen is a 58% reduction in sanctions over the last 6 years... so, yeah, that's a good place to start.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at a number (60,000) but avoids setting an actual target.

specificity.statement: From June, MSD will begin holding work [check-ins] that people will be required to attend if they've been on the job seeker benefit for 6 months.
specificity.explanation: Names a start month (June), a mechanism, and an eligibility threshold (6 months).

specificity.statement: This is expected to result in an additional 2 and 1/2 thousand job seekers each month having a work testable activity to [check in] on what they have been doing.
specificity.explanation: Quantified monthly impact (2,500 job seekers).

specificity.statement: With 70,000 more people now on job seeker support compared to when National left office 6 years ago. And about 40,000 more people have been receiving the support for a year or more.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures anchored to a defined timeframe.

specificity.statement: There is significant evidence that shows employment leads to a better way of life for people in terms of their financial stability, social connectedness, better health outcomes, and greater opportunities for themselves and their children.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete dimensions (financial, social, health) but no figures or studies.

specificity.statement: We're on record that we will not be changing the child poverty reduction act. We we worked I personally worked with the last government to ensure that we had a piece of legislation that the National Party in opposition could support and so that hasn't changed.
specificity.explanation: Clear on the commitment (no change) but defers the actual target-setting question.
